Quotes and footers are cut short, which conflicts with the no-truncation promise in the header.
Layout heights are estimates that may cause overlapping text.

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: File purpose and imports
sections.what: Describes the lessons deck format and what it is built from. It brings in the shared template kit, the deck types, a text-cleaning helper, and the data types for the recipe result.
sections.why: The header states the rules the deck must follow: claim-level sources, no truncation, and the shared Reality Scan tools.
sections.watch_out: Imports use long relative paths into another package, so moving these folders will break the build.

sections.name: STANCE, ED, Block
sections.title: Colours and labels for pillar stances
sections.what: Sets the four stance labels, strength, weakness, mixed and insufficient evidence, each with its own colour, symbol and label. It also sets a marker for editorial text and defines the shape of a layout block.
sections.why: Likely reason: the heat map and factbase need one shared way to show each stance.
sections.watch_out: The minus sign is written as an escape code, so retyping it as a plain hyphen changes how it looks.

sections.name: industryName
sections.title: Turning an industry code into a label
sections.what: Converts an industry code such as lng or real-estate into a readable name. Known codes have fixed names; any other code has its hyphens turned into spaces and its first letter capitalised.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond the fallback rule.
sections.watch_out: A new industry code with an unusual spelling will show as capitalised words unless it is added to the list of fixed names.

sections.name: paginate
sections.title: Splitting blocks into pages
sections.what: Takes a list of content blocks and packs them onto pages of a set height, starting a new page when the next block would not fit. A small gap separates blocks.
sections.why: The header says long sections continue onto extra slides so nothing is cut off.
sections.watch_out: A single block taller than the page still gets its own page and overflows, because nothing here shrinks it.

sections.name: place
sections.title: Positioning blocks on a slide
sections.what: Draws a list of blocks one below another from a starting position, moving down by each block's height plus a gap.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Blocks are placed without checking the bottom edge of the slide, so the caller must choose a page that fits.

sections.name: buildLessonsSceneDeck (part 1)
sections.title: Setting up names, lookups and citations
sections.what: Starts the main builder. It creates the timestamp, the industry label, and lookup tables for projects, facts, methodology items and sources. It removes bracketed notes from project names and defines how each fact or method item becomes a citation a reader can open.
sections.why: A comment says bracketed notes are internal annotations rather than real names, so they are removed from display names.
sections.watch_out: The citation quote for each fact is cut at 1600 characters, which conflicts with the header's no-truncation promise.

sections.name: buildLessonsSceneDeck (part 2)
sections.title: Small building blocks for text and bullets
sections.what: Defines reusable pieces: a paragraph, a titled body, a heading with a coloured rule, and a bullet with a dot. Each piece measures its own height so pages can be packed. A footer helper cuts source lines to 320 characters.
sections.why: Likely reason: the slides repeat many similar text pieces, and measuring height lets the pagination work.
sections.watch_out: Heights are estimates from the template's text measure, so if the estimate is off, text can overlap the block below.

sections.name: buildLessonsSceneDeck: if
sections.title: Executive summary and approach slides
sections.what: Builds the executive summary, with headline findings, the three most widespread failure modes, and four headline figures, spread over as many pages as needed. Then builds the approach slide, with study counts by outcome, the case selection rule, and five steps from the fact base to synthesis, each with a formula behind it.
sections.why: Likely reason: the deck opens with a summary and then explains how the numbers were produced.
sections.watch_out: Failure modes are ranked only by how many projects cite them, so ties keep their input order.

sections.name: buildLessonsSceneDeck (part 4)
sections.title: Framework and lessons table slides
sections.what: Draws a slide with one column per pillar, showing each pillar's principle and sub-drivers. Then draws a lessons table with pillar, lesson, recipe for success and failure modes, split over pages.
sections.why: Likely reason: summary tables let a reader compare pillars at a glance.
sections.watch_out: Once a framework column reaches the bottom of the page, the remaining sub-drivers are dropped silently, so a long framework can lose items without warning.

sections.name: buildLessonsSceneDeck (part 5)
sections.title: Per-pillar comparison slides
sections.what: For each pillar, builds one or more slides showing failure modes on the left and recipe practices on the right, under a band with the pillar name and principle. It also starts the heat map by setting its size and grouping the cases.
sections.why: Likely reason: the study compares what went wrong with what worked, one pillar at a time.
sections.watch_out: If a pillar has no cited items, a placeholder sentence is shown, so an empty pillar can look like a finished one.

sections.name: buildLessonsSceneDeck: for
sections.title: Heat map of cases against pillars
sections.what: Draws the heat map: one row per case, grouped into successful deliveries and cautionary tales, with the recorded outcome and a coloured cell for each pillar showing strength, mixed, weakness or no evidence. It splits into pages of nineteen rows and adds a colour legend.
sections.why: Likely reason: a grid lets the reader see patterns across many projects at once.
sections.watch_out: Nineteen rows per page is fixed, so taller rows would push the legend off the slide.

sections.name: buildLessonsSceneDeck: if
sections.title: Cross-case comparison and group dividers
sections.what: Draws a comparison table: for each pillar, counts of strength and weakness among successful projects and among cautionary tales, plus what separated them. It also defines the divider slides and the strip of coloured stance boxes, and starts a divider before each group of case profiles.
sections.why: Likely reason: the comparison answers the question of what separates success from failure.
sections.watch_out: Mixed and insufficient cases are left out of both counts, so a small group can look more decisive than it is.

sections.name: buildLessonsSceneDeck: for
sections.title: Case snapshot pages
sections.what: For each featured case, builds a snapshot with a name and performance line, a panel of project facts such as country, technology, budget and dates, and narrative blocks for outcome, context and timeline. Long narrative continues onto extra pages.
sections.why: Likely reason: each case needs a one-page overview before the detailed factbase.
sections.watch_out: The budget line shows 'latest' only when an actual budget exists and 'planned' otherwise, so a missing actual figure is labelled as a planned one.

sections.name: buildLessonsSceneDeck (part 9)
sections.title: Factbase pages per case
sections.what: For each featured case, builds pages of a table with one row per pillar: a stance chip, a written assessment, and what worked or went wrong. An 'Other / outcome' row holds notes that fit no pillar. Long tables continue onto extra pages.
sections.why: Likely reason: the snapshot is a summary, and this page gives the evidence behind each pillar.
sections.watch_out: The footer quotes the case's total admitted fact count, which may not match the number of rows shown.

sections.name: buildLessonsSceneDeck (part 10)
sections.title: Appendix, limits and closing slides
sections.what: Adds the appendix divider, then methodology source tables listing captured sources at thirteen per page, then an evidence-gaps slide listing held-back facts, thin pillars and dropped statements, and finally the thanks slide.
sections.why: Likely reason: a study has to state its own limits next to its claims.
sections.watch_out: The gaps slide's counts come from the run statistics, so if those statistics are wrong, the stated limits will be wrong too.

sections.name: buildLessonsSceneDeck (part 11)
sections.title: Saved project facts and the final deck object
sections.what: Builds a list of project facts for the assistant and the research tools, covering every case but keeping source links for only the first twelve facts of each. It removes inline citation markers from slide text, then returns the whole deck with its title, timestamps, caveat, and empty message and proposal lists.
sections.why: The comment says these facts are for the assistant and tools, and the marker removal handles inline alias lists left in older saved syntheses.
sections.watch_out: Tools see only the first twelve facts' sources for each project, so they get a partial list of evidence.

summary: Builds the Lessons Learnt slide deck, in the Reality Scan template format, from a finished recipe result, with a source behind each claim.
purpose: Turns the analysis of successful and cautionary projects into a slide deck that someone can edit, check against sources, and export.
why: The file header says every factual element must carry a source, that nothing is truncated, and that the deck uses the same editing and export tools as the Reality Scan deck.
how: 1. Builds lookup tables for projects, facts, methodology items and sources. 2. Defines small builders for text, bullets and headings that measure their own height. 3. Builds the cover and the executive summary. 4. Builds the approach, framework and lessons tables. 5. Builds the pillar comparison slides and the heat map. 6. Builds the cross-case comparison, then the case snapshot and factbase pages for each featured case. 7. Adds the appendix, methodology sources, evidence gaps and thanks slides. 8. Freezes project facts for the assistant and returns the deck object.
inputs: A finished `RecipeV3Result` and a run ID string.
outputs: A `ScanDeck` object holding slides, projects, a caveat, and empty message and proposal lists.
risks: The header says nothing is truncated, but quotes are cut at 1600 characters and footers at 320. Heights are estimates, so text can overlap. Stances are model-graded, and the deck itself calls them directional. The sources are only as good as the upstream checks.
debug: If a slide is empty, check the matching pillar lessons or case list in the input; empty lists produce placeholder text. If a citation shows as missing, check the claim's ids against the facts list. If layout overflows, check the height estimates and the page size constants such as BODY_BOTTOM.
